Five reply measurements, two context snapshots, and two memory snapshots. · Llama 3.1 8B Instruct · Q4_K_M · Unsloth Desktop **The fifth reply followed the reported context truncation, with a much longer Total but the same displayed generation rate.** Context fell from 7,247 to 3,148 tokens. M5 generated at **41.2 tok/s**, matching M4, while its displayed Total rose to **62.21 seconds**. ## At a glance - **Speed:** 64.6 → 60.5 → 61.6 → 41.2 → 41.2 tok/s. M5 is unchanged from M4 at displayed precision and 36.2% below M1. - **Waiting:** M5 produced 942 tokens in 22.85 seconds of backend Generation, but Total was 62.21 seconds, 40.8% higher than M4. The 39.36-second difference is not explained by the displayed 1.08-second prompt evaluation. - **Context:** used context fell from 7,247 / 8,192 (88.5%) after M4 to 3,148 / 8,192 (38.4%) after M5. The configured capacity stayed the same. - **Memory:** both supplied snapshots show RAM 27.6 / 31.9 GiB and VRAM 7.46 / 7.96 GiB. Matching rounded endpoints do not show what happened during the wait. **Evidence update:** all nine original screenshots have now been visually inspected and independently checked. The previous OCR discrepancies are resolved, including M2’s clearly displayed 60.5 tok/s. The original source inventory and reconciliation history are retained below. **Prompt/status record:** the user reports that the next prompt triggered context truncation and took a while. The three new images show timing, context, and memory only. The exact prompt text and a backend truncation log were not supplied.
Contents
## 1 · Test setup
Item Recorded setup
Model Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
Quantization Q4_K_M (downloaded GGUF)
Application Unsloth Desktop 0.1.905-beta; Studio/package version 2026.10.3
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060, 8 GB class; monitor reports 7.96 GiB
CPU AMD Ryzen 5 5600X
System memory 32 GB installed; monitor reports 31.9 GiB
Operating system Windows
Configured context 8K / 8,192 tokens
Test scope Five successive replies in one conversation, supplied in start-to-last order; M5 follows user-reported truncation
Hardware, model, and app settings come from the accompanying conversation; screenshot readings are identified separately below. This is a personal usage record, not a controlled cross-model benchmark. No new inference tests were run for this report. ## 2 · How much slower was each reply? ![](notion-file-block://a445fe4f-37eb-4e62-be45-cefa86c9c971/66fb3f8a-81c9-4833-aca8-a9b2c79c5859?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=01-generation-speed.png) ![](notion-file-block://8a347ff5-5db5-4630-99d3-458164061fbd/bb6d0bf6-94be-4b71-89fe-910e9aa4f7c3?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=02-step-changes.png)
Reply Speed (tok/s) Change vs previous (tok/s / %) Vs M1 ms per output token
M1 64.6 Baseline +0.0% 15.48
M2 60.5 -4.1 / -6.3% -6.3% 16.53
M3 61.6 +1.1 / +1.8% -4.6% 16.23
M4 41.2 -20.4 / -33.1% -36.2% 24.27
M5 † 41.2 +0.0 / +0.0% -36.2% 24.27
† M5 follows the user-reported truncation boundary. The marker locates it between observations, not at a verified elapsed timestamp. **Read the percentages with the right baseline.** M4 and M5 each retain 63.8% of M1’s displayed generation throughput. A 36.2% rate loss corresponds to about **56.8% more generation time for the same token count**, because time is the reciprocal of speed. M4 → M5 is 0.0% at the displayed precision. M2 is now directly confirmed as 60.5 tok/s, resolving the earlier OCR conflict. All rates remain rounded measurements. The sequence is not monotonic and provides no fitted slowdown curve or predictable threshold. The single post-truncation reply does not prove the reset had no effect on performance. ## 3 · Why a reply can take longer ![](notion-file-block://8946fdfa-5634-4658-b5a8-6d0c414c97eb/c395d8e0-7c36-48d3-b8dd-6cfe8edd0263?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=03-output-and-time.png)
Reply Output tokens Generation (s) Total (s) Total − Generation (s)
M1 1,173 18.15 18.39 0.24
M2 1,910 31.57 31.79 0.22
M3 2,160 35.05 35.21 0.16
M4 1,812 43.95 44.17 0.22
M5 942 22.85 62.21 39.36
- **M1 → M2:** output grew 62.8%, while generation speed fell 6.3%. Most of the extra generation time came from producing a longer answer. - **M2 → M3:** output grew 13.1%, while speed improved 1.8%. A longer answer still took longer overall. - **M3 → M4:** output shrank 16.1%, but generation time rose 25.4%. The lower generation rate outweighed the shorter response. - **M4 → M5:** output and generation time both fell about 48.0%, while displayed speed stayed at 41.2 tok/s. Despite the shorter answer, Total rose **18.04 seconds (+40.8%)**. - **M1 → M5:** output fell 19.7%; backend Generation rose 25.9%; displayed Total rose 238.3%. These compare different quantities, all against M1. The equal-length panel isolates throughput arithmetic: 1,000 output tokens corresponds to 15.48 seconds at M1’s rate and 24.27 seconds at the M4/M5 rate. These are generation-equivalent calculations, not extra test runs or full user-perceived latency. ### The additional wait on M5 ![](notion-file-block://c32c4352-1b9f-47eb-aeea-ba874c337ba7/01a35cec-547a-4c57-8d89-5f569920bd59?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=07-total-and-generation.png) **62.21 − 22.85 = 39.36 seconds.** M5’s displayed Prompt eval is only 1.08 seconds. Subtracting that as well leaves **38.28 seconds arithmetically unaccounted for by these displayed backend timings**. The earlier Total − Generation differences were only 0.16–0.24 seconds. **Do not label the whole gap “prefill,” “cache rebuild,” or “truncation time.”** Those are possible explanations to investigate, alongside work not captured by the final backend counters, but the screenshots do not identify the cause. No measured click-to-first-text duration is available. **Timing boundaries matter.** Generation is backend predicted time; Total is a client stream interval. They do not share proven identical start/end boundaries. Their differences are descriptive arithmetic, not a measured pipeline decomposition. [Exact-release timing adapter](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/blob/d94ca0ee6b54891378c6de65af9eba48f1afae59/studio/frontend/src/features/chat/api/chat-adapter.ts#L8419-L8427). ## 4 · Prompt processing and cache reuse ![](notion-file-block://154b25d9-7f09-43e2-83ff-b5ffb35186a1/5d30829d-e094-426f-a974-28e11aa3b6bd?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=04-prompt-and-cache.png)
Reply Prompt eval (ms) Prompt speed (tok/s) Cache hits (tokens) Displayed First token (ms)
M1 112 257.9 82 112
M2 44 812.5 1,283 44
M3 42 636.3 3,228 42
M4 55 381.7 5,414 55
M5 1,080 2,042.9 Not shown / unknown 1,080
**Prefill and decode are separate jobs.** Prompt eval and Prompt speed describe input processing. Speed describes output generation. M5’s 2,042.9 prompt tok/s is not its generation rate. Before the reported reset, cached tokens rose from 82 to 5,414. The first reply was already cache-warm, so it is not a demonstrated cold-start result. “Cache hits” counts reused prompt tokens, not GPU-cache bytes or a hit-rate percentage. M5’s prompt evaluation rose from M4’s 55 ms to **1,080 ms (about 19.6×)**. Its cache-hit row is absent in both supplied M5 panels; the count is **unknown, not a measured zero**. Rounded 1.08 s × 2,042.9 prompt tok/s ≈2,206 tokens, nearly the full displayed M5 prompt. That is consistent with substantial reprocessing after the reset, without proving exact zero cache reuse or explaining the much longer Total. **Important app-specific detail:** in this exact Unsloth release, completed GGUF messages overwrite displayed **First token** with backend prompt-evaluation time when available. That includes M5’s 1.08 seconds. These values are not independent measurements from clicking Send to seeing the first text. The release tag 0.1.905-beta maps to the code whose package version is 2026.10.3. This behavior was checked against that release. [Release](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/releases/tag/v0.1.905-beta), [version file](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/blob/d94ca0ee6b54891378c6de65af9eba48f1afae59/unsloth/_version.py), [completed-message assignment](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/blob/d94ca0ee6b54891378c6de65af9eba48f1afae59/studio/frontend/src/features/chat/api/chat-adapter.ts#L8418-L8429). ## 5 · Context: before and after the reported truncation ![](notion-file-block://01afaa2e-29c1-4825-bab6-860039f0dde6/355cf8e5-ea1c-4c1f-bd48-a9535c4aad9e?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=05-context-snapshot.png)
Snapshot component After M4 · S5 After M5 · S8
Full prompt 5,435 2,206
Of that prompt: cached prefix 5,414 Not shown / unknown
Newly processed prompt portion 21 (prompt − cache) ≈2,206 from rounded timing × rate; not exact
Completion 1,812 942
Used context 7,247 3,148
Configured capacity 8,192 8,192
Used share 88.5% 38.4%
Unused snapshot capacity 945 5,044
**Observed:** the later snapshot contains **4,099 fewer tokens**, a 56.6% reduction relative to the M4 endpoint, or **50.0 percentage points** of the same configured window (calculated from the unrounded token ratios). This supports the user’s report of context reduction/truncation. The snapshots do not show the exact discard/summary mechanism, which messages were removed, or the precise moment it happened. **The net decrease is not an exact count of tokens discarded.** The endpoints include different prompts and completions, and no request payloads or intermediate context history were captured. The exact triggering prompt text is not present in the uploaded images. **Do not double-count the cache.** M4 reconciles as 5,414 cached + 21 newly processed + 1,812 generated = 7,247. Its cached tokens are already inside the 5,435 prompt total. M5 independently reconciles as **2,206 prompt + 942 completion = 3,148**; no cache count is added or assumed. [llama.cpp accounting](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md#post-v1chatcompletions-openai-compatible-chat-completions-api). The 8,192 figure is configured capacity, not occupied tokens. The 5,044 remaining tokens are snapshot headroom, not a guaranteed next-answer allowance after new input, formatting, and backend reservations. Only these two context snapshots are plotted. There is no interpolated history. Growing occupied context can increase attention work even when KV buffers were already allocated; a reduced endpoint does not guarantee proportionally lower Windows-visible VRAM. [KV-cache allocation and active extent](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/50e3e3e480c80b9ee0ea067e475602d540dc62c8/src/llama-kv-cache.cpp#L231-L295). ## 6 · RAM and VRAM: matching endpoint snapshots ![](notion-file-block://da93cb10-2fbf-405f-a167-a969d6710631/830baf35-eb3f-423f-86f3-7fefa3684af5?space_id=1973bdb6-edb1-4c28-9480-b7a6ac2f9a4c&name=06-memory-snapshot.png)
Pool After M4 · S6 After M5 · S9 Calculated used Approx. headroom
System RAM 27.6 / 31.9 GiB 27.6 / 31.9 GiB 86.5% 4.3 GiB
GPU VRAM 7.46 / 7.96 GiB 7.46 / 7.96 GiB 93.7% 0.50 GiB
All GiB values are visually confirmed. The app displays RAM 86% and VRAM 94%; the chart uses percentages computed from rounded GiB values. RAM and VRAM are separate pools and their percentages must not be added. Both snapshots show limited headroom and identical rounded values. That does **not** establish that memory use stayed constant through the pause, that no transient spike occurred, or that no paging/offload occurred. These are whole-monitor readings rather than model-process allocation. There is no per-message memory trajectory or shared-GPU-memory measurement in the supplied images. Even a nonzero shared-memory value alone would not identify model spill. [Microsoft’s GPU-memory accounting explanation](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/directx/gpus-in-the-task-manager/). ## 7 · What the evidence supports
Statement Assessment
M5 generation throughput was lower than M1 Supported: 41.2 vs 64.6 tok/s, −36.2%
M5 generated more slowly than M4 Not shown: both display 41.2 tok/s
Every reply was slower than the previous reply Not supported: M3 recovered slightly, then M4/M5 match
M5 took longer only because it generated more text Not supported: output fell 48.0%, but Total rose 40.8%
Context was reduced around the reported truncation Supported by user report plus the lower context endpoint
Exactly 4,099 old tokens were discarded Not established: 4,099 is the net difference between two different endpoints
All 39.36 extra seconds were prefill or cache rebuilding Not established: displayed Prompt eval is 1.08 s; no stage trace
M5 had exactly zero cache hits Unknown: row is absent; rounded arithmetic is not an exact counter
VRAM spill, CPU offload, or thermal throttling caused the wait Unproven: no allocation, clocks, temperature, or stage logs
Matching memory endpoints rule out a transient problem Not supported: no measurements during the interval
This GPU/model performs poorly in general Too broad: this is five uncontrolled replies, no quality scoring or repeat tests
The strongest defensible interpretation is: **M5 followed a reported context truncation, showed a lower context endpoint and unchanged displayed decode rate, and had a much larger gap between client Total and backend Generation.** The screenshots support those observations but do not isolate the reset mechanism or latency cause. [NVIDIA’s prefill/decode explanation](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/).
8 · A cleaner follow-up test, if you choose to run one The useful question is whether the drop repeats at similar occupied context under otherwise stable conditions. 1. Keep the same model, quantization, application build, GPU layers, KV-cache types, batch settings, sampling settings, and output-token cap. Record the seed when supported. 2. Compare repeated short-, medium-, and long-context cases with comparable output length. Record both cold-cache and warm-cache cases separately. A fresh chat alone does not guarantee every backend cache is cold. 3. Capture raw backend timing/token counters and allocation/offload logs. Record app-process RAM, dedicated/shared GPU memory, GPU/CPU utilization, clocks, temperature, and power alongside each run. 4. Measure click-to-first-visible-text separately, because this release’s completed First token display is not that measure. 5. Change only one factor at a time: occupied context, configured capacity, or offload/KV settings. Raising the context limit is not itself a speed fix and may change memory requirements. 6. Report repeat variation and medians, not only the fastest run. Keep quality observations separate from throughput. These are suggested controls; no new test, setting change, or monitoring was performed.
9 · Methodology and limitations **Ordering:** M1–M5 follow the user’s stated order. The M4→M5 boundary is marked as user-reported truncation. Filename/import timestamps are not verified inference timestamps; there is no elapsed-time x-axis. **Extraction:** all nine source screenshots were visually inspected in this update and independently cross-checked. Old OCR disagreements are preserved as history, not unresolved numeric uncertainty. Source values remain rounded displays. **Calculations:** adjacent percent change = (current ÷ previous − 1) × 100; M1-relative changes use M1; ms/token and generation-equivalent seconds per 1,000 tokens = 1,000 ÷ tok/s; occupancy = used ÷ capacity × 100; headroom = capacity − used. Occupancy percentage-point change uses the difference in shares, not relative percentage change. **Scope:** n=5 conversational replies, two context endpoints and two memory endpoints, one setup, no repeats, confidence intervals, fitted curve, or causal intervention. Prompts/outputs differ. The actual prompt texts, generation timestamps, thermal/clock history, process allocation, raw backend counters and truncation logs are not supplied. **Metric definitions:** Speed/Generation use backend predicted counters; Prompt eval/Prompt speed use backend prompt counters. Tokens uses backend completion usage when available, otherwise an app estimate; Chunks counts stream chunks. First token is overwritten by prompt_ms on completion in this release. No independent click-to-first-visible-text measure is present. **Cross-checks:** output tokens ÷ generation seconds gives approximately 64.63, 60.50, 61.63, 41.23, and 41.23 tok/s, consistent with all displayed one-decimal rates. These extra decimals are calculations, not more precise measurements. **Unknowns:** M5 cache hits stay null/unknown. The net context decrease is not the exact discarded-token count. Total − Generation and Total − Generation − Prompt eval are descriptive differences across timing scopes, not identified pipeline stages. **Verification:** all seven generated charts are checked for values, labels, branding, and clipping. The page is read back after publication. The ZIP is checked against final PNG bytes and includes current data, calculation/render scripts, assets/licenses, source images, and a data guide.

M1 112 ms / 257.9 tok/s 18.15 s / 64.6 tok/s 1,173 / 82 112 ms / 18.39 s / 1,174

## Source-identity evidence and earlier design rationale
**Read with the October 7 policy review above.** The following retained September 24 analysis explains the existing protection and tradeoff; it does not pre-decide which refusals must remain hard failures.
### What was learned
The app currently revalidates source identity before/after encoding.
For Ahmed's long OBS recording, retained evidence showed:
- same path;
- same device/file ID;
- same size;
- same mtime;
- same birth/creation time;
- same sparse content fingerprint;
- different **ctime**.
A controlled test proved that harmless filesystem-attribute changes can alter ctime without altering file bytes.
A second controlled test proved that a real content edit outside sparse fingerprint windows can be constructed while preserving size/mtime/sampled bytes, leaving ctime as the remaining warning signal.
Therefore simply deleting ctime from the identity contract would weaken protection in a way that existing sparse sampling cannot safely replace.
### Product interpretation
This is not CIA-level authenticity protection.
The reason for source revalidation is ordinary consistency:
- a recording may still be growing;
- another app may replace or rewrite it;
- metadata may be edited;
- cloud/sync/indexing/tooling may touch the file;
- a long-running encode should not silently publish against a source whose identity became uncertain.
However, the application must **not become a digital-forensics product**.
Future design preference:
- keep meaningful fail-closed protection;
- improve human diagnostics;
- make retry/reprepare cheap;
- avoid whole-file hashing of tens of gigabytes merely to prove nothing changed;
- do not spend major future quota escalating identity complexity unless real field usage repeatedly demonstrates a need.
Potential future UX:
- exact changed-field explanation;
- “Re-inspect and retry” convenience;
- distinction between content-relevant and filesystem-metadata changes *only if* stronger evidence can justify it safely.
0.7 planning question:
> Is the current strict identity policy producing meaningful real-world friction often enough to justify a product change, or is better diagnostics/retry UX sufficient?

## Security — the project is stronger than the March mental model
Ahmed's lingering mental model is roughly:
> HTML/CSS/JS wrapper around FFmpeg.
That described the early prototype much better than the current application.
Current security architecture already includes important controls:
- sandboxed renderer;
- no renderer Node access;
- context isolation;
- narrow preload bridge;
- explicit named IPC methods;
- sender/top-level frame validation;
- payload/settings validation;
- main-owned filesystem paths;
- main-owned plan/queue/process authority;
- fixed FFmpeg/ffprobe binaries;
- argument arrays;
- `shell: false`;
- no renderer arbitrary executable choice;
- no renderer arbitrary argv submission;
- custom local `app://encoder` protocol;
- exact local asset allowlist;
- restrictive CSP;
- navigation / popup / permission denial;
- local media protocol restrictions;
- output validation before publication;
- no-overwrite publication;
- owned-only cleanup;
- bounded helper/process behavior.
This is meaningfully aligned with modern Electron security guidance.
Electron is not “secure because Electron” or “insecure because Electron.”
Its tradeoff is a larger bundled attack surface:
- Chromium;
- Node;
- Electron;
- npm dependencies;
- application JavaScript;
- FFmpeg parsers/codecs.
A native C++ application would have a different risk profile, including memory-safety and native parser risks. “Native” is not automatically safer.
The key architectural question is:
> **If renderer/UI content becomes compromised, what authority does it gain?**
The present architecture deliberately limits that authority.
## Security-left principle for future development
Ahmed wants security treated as part of design, not as a final checklist.
Carry this into all future milestones.
For every new feature, planning should ask:
- What new authority does this feature need?
- What new untrusted input does it parse?
- Does it add IPC?
- Does it expose a path, command, URL, executable or argument surface?
- Does it add dependencies?
- Does it broaden filesystem access?
- Does it create persistence/state?
- Can malformed media trigger dangerous behavior?
- Does it change update/distribution risk?
- What negative/security tests prove the boundary?
Security should be a **cross-cutting acceptance dimension**, not one isolated “security phase.”

### HDR → SDR tone mapping

Ahmed confirms that no dedicated application icon was created in earlier versions; it is missing, rather than an existing icon failing to apply. He dislikes the generic Electron-style appearance. Add creation and integration of a dedicated FFmpeg Encoder app icon as a 0.7 polish candidate.
The desired outcome is a recognizable application icon in normal Windows use. Visual design has not been chosen, and this note does not authorize implementation.
## October 7 polish request — About section
Add an About section as a 0.7 planning candidate so users can get a concise overview of the software they are using, as in a finished desktop application.
Ahmed requests:
- Application name and actual app version.
- Bundled FFmpeg version.
- Possibly contributor/creator credits explaining who worked on the application.
Exact layout and credit wording remain to be decided. Version information should reflect the actual packaged software rather than become stale manually maintained text. This records requested planning scope, not implementation authorization.
## October 7 UI polish constraints and recipe explanation
**Preserve existing functionality and guidance:** Ahmed explicitly says less visual density must not mean removing implemented features, controls, explanatory/info icons or existing guidance. Work with what exists and improve its presentation and clarity. Any proposed regrouping must preserve discoverability and access; removal is not part of this request.
**Concrete help-text improvement:** The hover explanation reached through the Blackwell Archive Quality recipe's info icon should describe what the recipe actually contains, not merely identify it as a recipe. Explain the settings in clear language, with enough detail for the user to understand their roles and tradeoffs.
**Known accepted recipe reference to verify against actual code/current UI before authoring:** HEVC NVENC, P7 preset, UHQ tuning, full-resolution multipass, VBR with CQ29 as an editable starting point, four B-frames and B-reference mode each. Distinguish UHQ tuning from CQ quality control and multipass; do not conflate these terms. Keep the recipe transparent and explain that CQ29 is a starting point, not universal x265 equivalence or a guaranteed output size.
Ahmed recalled some terms approximately during voice discussion. Use the verified implementation and actual displayed/current settings as the authority for exact wording, including any additional recipe settings not listed here. Preserve the explanation icon while improving the content and readable presentation. This is a requested planning improvement, not a request to change the encoding recipe.
**Broader rationale:** Dedicated polish should revisit small features and explanations that received limited attention while development focused on completing larger functional goals.
## October 7 design reference — Percentage Calculator section hover cue
**Owner preference and purpose:** Ahmed likes the subtle left-edge interaction cue in Percentage Calculator Tool v1.1. It draws his eyes toward the section under the mouse and helps him stay oriented in a dense interface without adding permanent visual clutter. Consider an analogous cue during FFmpeg 0.7 UI planning; exact placement and colors remain design decisions.
**Exact source reference:** G:/AI Directed Software Development/Percentage Calculator Tool (Finished Project)/Percentage Calculator Tool v1.1.html.
**Verified code behavior:** In lines 46–52, .calc-section has a permanent 2px amber/yellow left border, color #E9A715. In lines 54–56, .calc-section:hover changes the left border to soft green, #94C59A, with a 120ms transition. Hovering anywhere within the section triggers the change. The section does not gain a glow or shadow, and this is not a section focus or active-state rule. A separate green input-focus outline exists and initially appears on the first field; distinguish it from the section hover accent.
**Interpretation for the dedicated FFmpeg thread:** Reuse the principle of a restrained, theme-consistent section hover accent that quietly indicates pointer context. Do not interpret Ahmed's earlier approximate description of illumination as a request for a large glow, or assume the original cue appears from nothing. Adapt to FFmpeg's actual layout and ensure keyboard focus remains understandable.
**Evidence limit:** Original HTML/CSS inspected read-only. A visual preview was attempted but supported local browser automation could not open local HTML files; no rendered screenshot or observed hover was obtained. This is a source-confirmed reference, not visually verified appearance. No calculator edits or FFmpeg implementation performed.
# 6. Future candidates and scope boundaries
The following remain candidates rather than commitments unless Ahmed deliberately promotes them:
- AMD AMF and Intel QSV implementations
- Scaling/resolution controls, including the discussed 4K60 → 1080p60 output using the normal recipe; not expressly promoted into current 0.7 scope
- Multi-resolution output ladders
- Convert / Extract / Remux workspace and audio conversion/extraction
- Installer/updater, public release and broader 1.0 work
**Already promoted as planning directions:** HDR research/design and a dedicated later whole-interface polish pass. This does not approve implementation or promise delivery of every HDR format within 0.7. The original broader deferral list is preserved as historical rationale in section 8.
# 7. Evidence gaps, decisions and handoff
## Evidence to collect when the work is approved
- Exact Resolve sample path, export settings and error text; inspect stream/container/color/metadata evidence before attributing a cause
- Exact TV-show sample, title/path/format and refusal reason; do not merge its diagnosis with Resolve or the fixed Samsung issue
- Screenshot and exact wording of the CPU-only laptop’s startup diagnostics
- Representative media fixtures that can legally/practically be retained without storing personal full recordings in Git
- Actual current implementation and UI settings before writing recipe help text
- Current UI and reviewable visual proposals for Ahmed; the calculator cue is code-confirmed, not visually verified
## Decisions still required
- Which inspection/preservation rules remain hard failures, become warnings or explicit choices, or can accept equivalent representations?
- Which media families, security checklist, runtime versions and independent-machine checks define a bounded 0.7 plan?
- What initial HDR formats/paths are feasible, and what separate research, benchmark and implementation gates apply?
- How should technical completion and owner-approved visual completion be tested separately?
- When should private GitHub be created, what may be uploaded, and what logs/data must be sanitized?
- What time/quota limit and freeze/park criteria keep the work proportional?
## Mother Thread / Codex handoff guidance for later
Future Jerry should:
1. read accepted 0.6 Current State / final M Execution Summary;
2. read this page;
3. review any new field feedback since 0.6 acceptance;
4. inspect the Product Backlog;
5. distinguish “stability requirement” from “new feature request”;
6. draft a bounded 0.7 product objective;
7. have Codex Plan Mode independently inspect architecture/security implications;
8. reconcile both plans with Ahmed before execution.
Future Codex should **not** treat this page as autonomous execution authorization.
It should use this as design input only after Ahmed explicitly approves a 0.7 Goal/Plan.
**Handoff update:** reconcile the original handoff steps with the current benchmark dependency, critical HDR planning track, proportional-policy review, later iterative UI pass and current no-separate-ctime-patch preference. Do not turn the historical detection/refusal-only endpoint into the new acceptance contract.
# 8. Foundations and historical rationale
**How to read this section:** the dated material preserves why earlier decisions were made. Where it conflicts with October 7 direction, the current topic sections above take precedence. In particular, default HDR deferral, refusal-only HDR acceptance, the separate ctime-patch option and avoidance of a broad UI pass are no longer the current planning assumptions.
## Why this page exists
Ahmed has now seen direct evidence that long-running development threads are fragile:
- a chat can reach practical length limits;
- a thread can fail;
- quota interruptions can split work across days;
- subagent work can survive while parent documentation lags;
- human memory fades quickly across dense development cycles.
Therefore long-lived projects need external durable memory that does not depend on one chat thread.
For FFmpeg Encoder specifically, the project may continue across months or years. The goal is to make each major version a clean, recoverable foundation so future work can resume from:
- Git;
- Current State / Continuation State;
- dated Execution Summaries;
- Notion project pages;
- Session Summaries;
- accepted artifact/tag evidence;
- explicit future-planning notes such as this page.
local-v0.6.0 is now accepted. This page should be read after Ahmed has had some normal-use time with the accepted artifact and any new field observations are available.
## The product transition after 0.6
0.5 established the modern foundation.
0.6 evolved that foundation into a real archive workflow:
- inspection reuse;
- safe same-folder operation;
- provenance/generated-output recognition;
- intentional re-encoding;
- remembered workflow;
- compact large-batch UI;
- transparent FFmpeg arguments;
- Archive Quality NVENC;
- field-QA fixes;
- stronger compatibility evidence;
- portable integrated acceptance.
The next useful question is no longer:
> **What large feature can we add next?**
The better question for 0.7 is:
> **Can Ahmed trust the application enough that normal use stops requiring him to think about its internals?**
This suggests a deliberate stabilization phase before AMD/QSV/scaling/conversion-workspace expansion.
## Candidate 0.7 identity
Working title:
> **FFmpeg Encoder 0.7 — Compatibility, Reliability & Security**
This is a *planning direction*, not approved scope.
Possible product thesis:
> Turn 0.6 from a highly capable locally accepted encoder into a broader, boringly reliable foundation across representative real-world media, long-running use, failure modes, security boundaries, and clean-machine operation.
The desired outcome is confidence, not feature count.
## Product philosophy learned from field QA
Real-world use found issues that hundreds of direct/native/packaged checks did not represent.
Examples:
- Samsung screen-recording MP4s exposed Matroska track-level timestamp preservation behavior.
- A multi-hour OBS recording exposed the practical consequences of strict source-identity checks.
- Real gameplay foliage/grass exposed quality loss that the earlier short Archive Quality benchmark underweighted.
Lesson:
> **Synthetic/unit/native acceptance evidence is necessary but cannot replace field use.**
A mature loop should be:
```plain text
automated tests
→ native/integration acceptance
→ packaged-artifact acceptance
→ real-world owner use
→ new representative regression fixtures
→ future regression protection
```
0.7 planning should deliberately include a small field-compatibility corpus derived from actual failure classes.
## September 24 update — 0.6 prerequisite satisfied
<callout icon="✅" color="green_bg">
	**local-v0.6.0 is now accepted.** The amended J–M Goal has closed after independent final M review found no unresolved approved blocker and the parent synchronized the living documentation. This planning page may now be used as future 0.7 design input — but it still does **not** authorize 0.7 implementation.
</callout>
Accepted 0.6 anchor for future planning:
- production source checkpoint: `7b41c0f`;
- current direct checks: **281**;
- fresh portable ZIP: **321,231,543 bytes**;
- ZIP SHA-256: `3b7c72ea3252dd9c3fff2d83227e3b5b04badf642b748c606063e339ead6f5bb`;
- packaged acceptance: **20 cases / 4 process sessions / 25 protected files**;
- independent final M review: **ACCEPT**, no blocking engineering gap;
- ordinary 0.5 artifact/tag remains preserved.
Recommended next phase remains: **normal owner use → collect field observations → inspect Git/private-GitHub readiness → deliberate 0.7 Plan Mode → Ahmed approval → execution.**
## September 24 HDR baseline and default deferral — superseded in scope
The current product is intentionally SDR-first.
Current detection already distinguishes:
- PQ / SMPTE ST 2084;
- HLG / ARIB STD-B67;
- recognized Dolby Vision evidence;
- HDR10+ dynamic metadata;
- ambiguous/incomplete color evidence;
- 10-bit SDR.
Important principle:
> **10-bit is not HDR. BT.2020 primaries alone are not HDR.**
Current desired behavior for true HDR is generally:
- detect it;
- explain it;
- refuse unsupported HDR rather than silently producing a damaged/incorrect SDR or falsely tagged output.
That is a *good* foundation behavior.
Future HDR work should be split conceptually:
### HDR → HDR preservation
Retain correct HDR signal through:
- codec/profile/bit depth;
- transfer function;
- primaries/matrix;
- static HDR metadata where applicable;
- dynamic metadata where applicable;
- playback/container signaling.
### HDR → SDR tone mapping
Actually transform the picture:
- map highlight range;
- convert transfer/color behavior;
- produce deliberate SDR;
- tag output honestly as SDR.
These are different features and must not be conflated.
Likely 0.7 stability approach:
- add real iPhone HDR/Dolby Vision and perhaps HDR10/HLG fixtures;
- prove detection and *safe refusal*;
- improve user-facing reason/help;
- defer actual HDR preservation/tone mapping to a later dedicated milestone unless Ahmed explicitly promotes it.
## September 24 expansion boundaries — updated by October 7 HDR and UI direction
Do not automatically fold these into 0.7 merely because they are attractive:
- AMD AMF implementation;
- Intel QSV implementation;
- scaling/resolution controls;
- multi-resolution output ladders;
- Convert / Extract / Remux workspace;
- audio conversion/extraction;
- full HDR preservation;
- HDR tone mapping;
- installer/updater;
- large UI redesign;
- public release;
- broad 1.0 work.
Some may eventually be promoted, but stabilization should remain coherent.
## September 24 planning pillars and acceptance seed — not an approved contract
When the weekly quota and human attention are available, build the formal plan around a small number of pillars:
1. **Compatibility matrix / regression corpus**
2. **Long-running reliability & soak testing**
3. **Security-left architecture/audit**
4. **Failure UX & diagnosability**
5. **Clean-machine / independent environment acceptance**
6. **GitHub/private remote workflow**
7. **Freeze / park criteria**
A possible endpoint:
> 0.7 is accepted when representative real-world SDR media behaves predictably, unsupported HDR/media fails clearly, no major security-boundary regression is found, long-running/batch workflows remain stable, a clean environment can run the portable app, and the repository is recoverable/inspectable remotely.
This sentence is a planning seed, not an approved acceptance contract.
## September 24 questions — retained with subsequent answers above
When returning later, explicitly decide:
- Does source-identity behavior need a policy change, or only better retry UX?
- Which real-world media families matter most to Ahmed?
- Can we legally/practically keep tiny owned regression excerpts, or should fixtures be generated?
- Should actual iPhone SDR + HDR media be acquired for testing?
- Should HDR in 0.7 be only detection/refusal verification?
- Which Electron version should 0.7 pin to?
- Should FFmpeg remain 9.0.1 or move only if security/compatibility evidence justifies it?
- What security standard/checklist will Codex audit against?
- Do we want a separate threat-model document?
- What constitutes clean-machine acceptance?
- Should private GitHub happen immediately after 0.6 or as the first 0.7 infrastructure milestone?
- What information from terminal logs must be excluded/sanitized before remote storage?
- What is the maximum amount of time/quota worth spending before declaring the foundation “good enough” and parking the project?
## September 24 sequencing — refined by later updates
Do not automatically start 0.7 immediately when 0.6 closes.
Preferred sequence:
```plain text
use/inspect accepted local-v0.6.0 normally
→ gather concrete field feedback for a short period
→ review this page
→ inspect real Git history
→ decide private GitHub timing
→ create a dedicated 0.7 Goal
→ Plan Mode / architecture + security review
→ Ahmed reviews the plan
→ execute only after approval
```
This creates a clean version boundary rather than carrying unfinished 0.6 momentum directly into an uncontrolled 0.7 expansion.
## September 26 benchmark sequence — ctime-patch option now superseded
Before approving encoder/default/Archive Quality changes inside 0.7, complete or deliberately narrow the dedicated benchmark campaign defined in <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3e7bd7ade63b8184b7e5c13bbb2cfabd"/>.
The intended order is now:
```plain text
accepted 0.6 normal use
→ dedicated encoder benchmark laboratory
→ interpret evidence / Ahmed subjective review
→ decide whether a bounded 0.6.1 ctime patch happens separately
→ formal 0.7 planning
→ product implementation only after approval
```
The benchmark must remain research-only and should not silently mutate accepted 0.6 product behavior.
**Editorial note:** two equivalent September 26 benchmark-sequencing entries were consolidated into this one; the benchmark reference and research-only boundary are unchanged.
## Long-term lesson
The FFmpeg project is no longer a short coding experiment.
It has become a long-lived software project with:
- versioned releases;
- regression history;
- user field feedback;
- security boundaries;
- artifact acceptance;
- product decisions;
- quality benchmarks;
- rollback points;
- durable documentation.
That means the project should mature like real software:
> stable foundation → field use → observed problems → bounded iteration → evidence → release → pause → later expansion
rather than:
> continuously add features until complexity becomes unmanageable.
<callout icon="🧠" color="gray_bg">
	**Core planning principle for 0.7:** favor confidence over breadth. The best 0.7 may add very few glamorous features if it makes 0.6 boringly reliable, understandable, secure-by-design, compatible with representative real media, and easy to resume years later.
</callout>
</content>
</page>

**Updated:** <mention-date start="2026-10-09"/> · Cairo dates and times unless stated otherwise.
**Prepared by:** Blue, with Ahmed, for the established ChatGPT mother thread, Jerry.
This is the current handoff for work Ahmed and Blue have done around the Freelancing Arc. It should let Jerry resume accurately if Blue is unavailable. It complements the full session summaries; it does not replace the Arc’s history, the live Opportunity Registry, or the durable core documents.
## Start here
**Claude’s foundation orientation, roadmap and Registry vocabulary, Natural Wholesale assessment, draft-to-submission comparison, final clarification, and historical Session Summary reading/reconciliation are complete.** Integration remains **Active**. Ahmed confirmed Failure Intelligence reading complete in voice on October 9. The two remaining operational steps are the read-only hub walkthrough and a reviewed first job-search/Registry trial when Ahmed starts that work.
**History-read evidence:** Claude reports reaching all 18 entries from March 24 through October 7 and checking the supplied text against the Project copy (15,186 lines; 433,772 bytes). It reported matching headings and ending, with no truncation. This checkpoint rests on Claude’s read log and synthesis; it is not independent verification of exhaustive reading or a second line-by-line disk read. No operational assignment began.
**Current stopping point:** Failure Intelligence reading is **complete, confirmed by Ahmed** in voice on <mention-date start="2026-10-09"/>. Blue has not independently inspected Claude’s final read report; no detailed reconciliation findings are claimed here. This supersedes the earlier quota-limit uncertainty. Resume with the read-only practical hub walkthrough.
**Read this handoff next for navigation.** The historical summary ends October 7 and does not contain the later October 8 work or Blue’s contribution. This handoff bridges that gap before the read-only Home/Registry walkthrough.
The most current integration status is <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3f0bd7ade63b81b98b15ee4c7e389295"/>. Current checklists in Home and the staged working page have been reconciled to Ahmed’s October 9 Failure Intelligence completion confirmation; explicitly dated earlier plans remain historical.
## What Blue actually contributed
### September 30 and early continuity
Blue’s role was established as a coordinator across Ahmed’s existing projects. The Freelancing Arc already had Jerry’s mother-thread work, source documents, proposal history and Notion system. Blue’s orientation did not create those foundations.
The distinction matters: reading or discussing Jerry’s completed work is not evidence that Blue performed it. This handoff credits Blue’s later orientation, coordination and Claude-calibration work separately from the Arc’s earlier construction, proposal submission and market scouting.
### October 6 task capture
Shortly after midnight on <mention-date start="2026-10-06"/>, Ahmed asked Blue to record Claude integration as an important active project after finding Claude useful in his Notion/Obsidian work. Blue created the existing integration record with:
- Active status
- Critical priority
- Very High AI Leverage
- Very Heavy Cognitive Load
The purpose was to add an independent collaborator and reduce coordination burden, with account capabilities and access limits to be tested rather than assumed. This was a project-task addition, not an Opportunity Registry job addition.
Source: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3f0bd7ade63b81b98b15ee4c7e389295"/>.
### October 7 deep grounding
At Ahmed’s request, Blue read the Arc’s five foundation documents and the complete Session Summary chronologically, oldest to newest. Blue’s completion report records six documents and eighteen dated sessions, through October 6–7.
This changed the basis for the subsequent Claude discussion. The Arc is an income-first career project, with skills and personal growth as supporting goals. Customer support is the current entry route. The profile, simulated portfolio, documentation and market-management system are usable foundations; the next progress comes from real opportunities and evidence, rather than repeatedly rebuilding setup.
Blue also connected that project understanding with the separate AI-model research. The resulting October 8 recommendation was to begin with the available Free Claude setup instead of making a paid subscription a prerequisite. A later upgrade can be justified by demonstrated usefulness, repeated interruption of meaningful work, or a deliberate need for sustained strategic collaboration. This was a dated practical recommendation, not proof that different models or plans are interchangeable.
The full Arc history remains in the [canonical Session Summary mirror](https://drive.google.com/file/d/19Mxurl3NQ4a9GI9SHZZhTrYHc-m_y3qG/view). Blue’s own session documentation records the October 7 immersion separately.
### October 8 guided Claude onboarding
Ahmed operated Claude and brought its responses back to Blue. Blue prepared bounded prompts, checked their outputs against sources, identified corrections and helped decide when a stage was complete.
**Foundation orientation passed.** Claude understood the ordering of goals, existing phase, Ahmed’s authority and the separation of durable rules, live state and history. One correction was important: Claude must preserve continuity of its own contributions through checkpoints and session notes, while Jerry remains the established whole-project partner. It should not create a competing project history.
**Roadmap and vocabulary passed.** Claude read the Roadmap and relevant Home content. It correctly distinguished Stage, Fit, Priority, Freshness, Client Risk, Tool Gap and Time Fit. The precision correction concerned Phase 5: completing an engagement alone is insufficient. The roadmap also requires real delivery evidence, emerging client feedback or review evidence, and improved judgment for future selection.
**Natural Wholesale was used as historical calibration.** This was deliberately split into two passes:
1. Read the original saved client listing and make an independent assessment before reading the detailed prior interpretation.
2. Compare Ahmed’s raw reasoning, Jerry’s drafts, Ahmed’s edits, the submitted build and the relevant simulated portfolio evidence.
This was not fully blind, since foundation material had already exposed some Natural facts. It was still useful for testing whether Claude could reason from primary material rather than echo the earlier match analysis.
**Blue distinguished Draft 1.1 from the final submitted build.** The final build includes the Pacific-overlap and split-check-in sentence added during submission checks. The historical drafting page’s blank application-material placeholders are not proof of unanswered screening questions.
**Claude’s final clarification was accepted on October 8.** It revised or narrowed weak criticisms for stated reasons, preserved a useful systems-experience question, and retained the concern about practical customer-update timing. No additional calibration round is needed.
## What the calibration taught us
These are working principles to preserve in future collaboration, not instructions to rewrite the submitted Natural proposal.
- **Keep preferences and requirements distinct.** The original listing’s twice-daily check-ins were introduced as “Ideally.” Some later interpretations strengthened that into a mandatory structure or prohibition on continuous work. The original source governs the claim. Clarify actual coverage before making future commitments.
- **Undocumented experience is not proven inability.** Lack of evidence about inbox ownership or B2B work should remain an unknown, not automatically become a demonstrated capability gap.
- **Professional, clear and human is Ahmed’s intentional voice.** He does not want unnecessary familiarity or friendliness added as a substitute for authenticity. Restrained language can be human. Critique clarity and effect, rather than assuming a warmer alternative must be better.
- **Selective emphasis is deliberate.** Ahmed wanted to disclose the WooCommerce gap, then emphasize relevant work and willingness to learn. Omitting his approximately six-month Amazon tenure was not automatically a defect. Additions must earn their place in a proposal.
- **Transferable work is not tool equivalence.** Relevant order-support experience can support a learning claim. We have not established that Amazon’s AC3 system is equivalent to WooCommerce. Describe actual actions and judgment rather than inventing direct platform mastery.
- **Judge simulated evidence against the claim actually made.** “Shows how I approach” investigation and follow-up is narrower than claiming completed real-world execution or a real customer outcome. The portfolio is openly simulated.
- **The birthday was acknowledged.** The portfolio reply explicitly referred to the son’s upcoming birthday. The remaining useful criticism concerns handling that urgency with a practical next step or timeframe, not an absence of acknowledgment.
- **A promised update still needs operational support.** Avoid unsupported delivery promises, but do not assume any update deadline is safe. Coverage, workflow and authority must support it.
- **Preserve the availability evidence boundary.** Blue reported recovering earlier context that Ahmed had confirmed general Pacific overlap and split check-ins before submission. Exact windows remained unresolved. Claude did not personally find that confirmation in its supplied packet; the packet’s documentation gap remained a valid finding.
Ahmed’s clarification and Blue’s review on October 8 are the source of these calibration outcomes. The source documents below preserve the historical wording and versions. Their earlier text has not been silently rewritten to erase the learning.
## Did Blue add jobs to the Opportunity Registry
**Resolved with Ahmed on October 8: these historical job additions were made in the Freelancing Arc mother thread with Jerry, not by Blue.** Ahmed recognized them as part of the earlier Arc and documentation-system work used for Claude’s grounding.
The September 30 Arc history explicitly says Ahmed asked **Jerry** to perform the livestream scout. Five opportunities were added after checking the twenty-three existing records:
- Async ecommerce email response support
- Ecommerce SaaS support operator
- Shopify support VA
- Morgan Systems customer experience
- Fountain Gifts service / VA
The October 6 audit records eight further additions: four saved during an interrupted attempt and four during the retry. The retry entered with thirty-two records and ended with thirty-six. Its documented sample was seventy-two unique job IDs, with zero authenticated Upwork reads. Those are historical research counts, not a new search performed for this handoff.
**Attribution readback on October 8:** all thirty-six current records include **🤖 Jerry** in **🤖 Scout**; Proposal #1 additionally includes **👤 Ahmed**. None is tagged Blue or ChatGPT. Home’s Scout legend lists Ahmed, Jerry, Gemini, Claude and Codex. The historical archive calls the market work Jerry’s. Blue’s reviewed conversation history did not provide a verified contrary execution record.
**Created-time check, distinct from edit time:** the newest four job records were created on October 6 at 4:22:02 PM Cairo: weekend SaaS, car-storage SaaS, Saura and Norwegian booking. The preceding four were created on October 6 at 3:39:49 PM Cairo: DLAB, phone/email operations, Shopify part-time and CML. The September 30 five were created at 6:05:03 PM Cairo. The complete thirty-six-row query contained **no job record created on October 7 or October 8 Cairo**.
**Clarification history:** Ahmed initially recalled that very recent additions might be Blue’s. After the creation dates and source history were checked, he explicitly corrected that recollection: these jobs belonged to the mother-thread work. The earlier uncertainty is closed. An edit timestamp alone must not be treated as a new job addition.
**Prospective attribution requirement from Ahmed:** if Blue adds jobs in future authorized work, create and use an explicit **Blue** naming tag for those contributions, with a clear signoff identifying what Blue actually did. Do not attribute Blue’s work to Jerry merely because both are OpenAI assistants. Preserve other collaborators’ contributions accurately.
Therefore:
- Keep the existing Jerry attribution for these historical jobs; no retroactive relabeling is needed.
- Distinguish Blue’s future additions from reading, reviewing or coordinating another collaborator’s records.
- Use the same shared Registry and duplicate controls; attribution does not require a parallel job list.
- The prospective attribution instruction is not an instruction to search for or add jobs now.
- No Scout tags, Registry schema or historical job entries were changed by this handoff.
Sources: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3d9bd7ade63b81d4b249f6e9957339be"/>, <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3f1bd7ade63b8140b59ff99624039a06"/>, the Session Summary mirror, and <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/00be3c9d984b44d9a4055070be3b3007"/>.
## Current operational state
These are the latest documented states checked for this handoff, not freshly observed Upwork-account facts.
- **Phase 4 remains active.** No first hire or client-delivery milestone was established in this handoff.
- **Natural Wholesale remains Submitted.** It was submitted on September 26 at 2:07 AM Cairo at US\$12 per hour, using twenty-two Connects with no boost. Its current personal outcome remains unverified. Preserve the submitted letter.
- **Pokémon is Skipped / Pass / Retired.** Historical Strong Fit remains accurate. No proposal was submitted and no Connects were spent. Its prior preparation is historical or optional practice; it must not resume automatically.
- **Latest documented balance is 106 Connects**, reported by Ahmed on October 6 at approximately 3:20 PM Cairo. This is not a fresh account read. Do not invent a reward, purchase or other explanation for the difference from the September 26 balance.
- **Fit Map is the primary visual work surface.** Current Review is the compact pre-application table; Freshness Map and All Opportunities preserve older research.
- **One job exists once.** Different collaborators use the same Registry. Fit describes the work; Freshness describes evidence and present visibility; Stage describes the relationship; Priority describes the next attention decision.
- **No current proposal target or new spending commitment is created here.** Logged-in checks are still needed before application decisions on public discoveries.
Source: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3e0bd7ade63b81789097d1e1181cccb9">The Freelancing Arc</mention-page> and its linked Registry. The current Claude checklist reflects Ahmed’s October 9 Failure Intelligence completion confirmation above; older dated onboarding plans remain historical.
## Authoritative reading route
1. **This handoff and the current integration record:** recover Blue’s contribution and the exact Claude stopping point. <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3f0bd7ade63b81b98b15ee4c7e389295"/>.

Review the actual additions or updates and attribution. This is planned work, not executed or authorized by this handoff.
5. **Preserve the result.** Update this same handoff with dated done/planned/unknown status and the next step, alongside a substantive session summary when requested. Do not create a second Registry or duplicate handoff page.
